# Proposal: Practitioner Academy for Tamarack Instruments

**To:** Dana Whitfield, General Counsel
**Program:** Practitioner Academy, AI Governance Academy
**Format:** 2 days, live virtual, four 90-minute working sessions per day
**Price:** US$12,500

## 1. Situation Summary

Tamarack Instruments designs and manufactures laboratory measurement instruments. It is headquartered in the Netherlands, operates in the Netherlands, Germany and the United States and has about 1,100 staff. Its AI maturity is at the piloting stage. It has three AI use cases:

* **Deployed:** a customer service chatbot on the support portal.
* **Piloting:** AI visual inspection on the German production line.
* **Planned:** AI sales forecasting next year.

The Client's regulatory drivers are the EU AI Act and GDPR. Work toward ISO/IEC 42001 is to start next year, and the start date is not fixed. The Client's incumbent frameworks are an ISO/IEC 27001 ISMS, an ISO 9001 quality management system and an internal audit function. An internal audit finding in June 2026 recorded that there is no inventory of AI systems.

Dana Whitfield has stated the objective directly: "I want governance in place before visual inspection goes into production in Q2 2027."

## 2. Why Hands-On Practitioner Capability Fits Now

The Practitioner Academy does not hand the Client a governance program. It builds the capability to produce one, using the Client's own AI use cases as the working material. Four facts make the timing relevant:

* The June 2026 finding names a specific missing artifact. Starting the inventory is a Day 1 exercise.
* The Q2 2027 production date for visual inspection sets a horizon for governance on a named system.
* The chatbot is deployed, so its governance is current work rather than planning.
* ISO/IEC 42001 work is expected next year, and practitioners who already work in structured repositories can carry that work forward.

The program teaches three principles: Slow AI, Informed Intent and Final Liability rests with the Human. Participants work directly in two repositories:

* GRC Workbook (https://github.com/rolldabones/grc-workbook)
* Slow AI Kitchen (https://github.com/rolldabones/slow-ai-kitchen)

Two further repositories serve as references:

* AI Governance for Boards (https://github.com/rolldabones/ai-governance-for-boards), for the board layer.
* The Definition of Done (https://github.com/rolldabones/definition-of-done), for the acceptance layer.

## 3. Running Worked Examples

Two use cases run through both days. The third enters on Day 1 only.

* **AI visual inspection (piloting).** This is the system named in the stated objective. Its link to production staff brings in the constraint that the German works council is consulted before anything touches production staff. That constraint makes the oversight and workflow design concrete.
* **Customer service chatbot (deployed).** This is the only system in use. The constraint that customer data must stay in the EU, together with GDPR, gives the governed prompting and evidence exercises real boundaries.
* **AI sales forecasting (planned).** This system enters the inventory and classification exercise only. It tests the intake procedure on a system before it is built.

**Confidentiality approach.** No real customer data is used in any exercise. Chatbot exercises use a sanitized analog: synthetic support queries written for the session. Visual inspection exercises use a sanitized process description with no images, names or data relating to production staff.

## 4. Curriculum Spine With Client Exercises

Module and pattern names below follow the program's curriculum spine. Exact repository file paths will be confirmed in the pre-work packet.

**Day 1: GRC Workbook. *The Turtle and the Phoenix* is told in Session 1 to seat the doctrine before the instruments arrive on Day 2.**

| Session | Exercise | Repository asset | Artifact produced |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | The fable is told from the facilitation kit (https://github.com/rolldabones/AI-Governance-Academy/blob/main/the-turtle-and-the-phoenix.md). The handle map then links the story to each workbook module, annotated with the visual inspection and chatbot examples. | Facilitation kit, handle map | Handle-to-module map for the two worked examples |
| 1 | Decision rights for the two worked examples, including escalation to the board layer | GRC Workbook, governance structures module, with AI Governance for Boards as reference | Draft decision-rights map, with owner fields completed by the Client |
| 1 | The kit's twenty-minute closing exercise, run at the close of the session | Facilitation kit, section 8 | The three artifacts specified in section 8 of the kit |
| 2 | Start the inventory with the chatbot, visual inspection, sales forecasting and systems participants bring. Classification fields are recorded as drafts for review by the Client. | GRC Workbook, AI system inventories and classification module | Started AI system inventory |
| 3 | Assess candidate risks for visual inspection (works council consultation, effect on production staff) and for the chatbot (EU data residency, GDPR) | GRC Workbook, risk and impact assessments module | Draft risk register entries and draft impact assessments |
| 4 | Draft an AI use policy section and an inventory intake procedure, written so the Client can consider alignment with its ISO 9001 quality management system and ISO/IEC 27001 ISMS | GRC Workbook, policies and operating procedures module | Draft policy section and intake procedure |

**Day 2: Slow AI Kitchen plus assurance**

| Session | Exercise | Repository asset | Artifact produced |
|---|---|---|---|
| 5 | Write governed prompts for the chatbot against the sanitized analog. Each prompt carries an authorization stating purpose, authority, boundaries and exit. | Slow AI Kitchen, governed prompting pattern | Governed prompt set with Informed Intent authorization record |
| 6 | Design two workflows: (1) chatbot escalation to a human, and (2) visual inspection decision handling, with works council consultation as a gate | Slow AI Kitchen, practical AI workflow design pattern | Two governed workflows |
| 7 | Attach each material outcome in both workflows to a named-owner field, with oversight and intervention points | Slow AI Kitchen, human oversight and accountability pattern | Oversight and accountability map |
| 8 | Define the evidence each workflow must produce. Test each workflow against the three Slow AI tests. Set acceptance criteria. | Slow AI Kitchen, evidence collection and audit readiness pattern, with The Definition of Done as reference | Evidence plan and acceptance criteria per workflow |

The principles are applied in their doctrine form:

* **Slow AI:** AI that cannot be governed, explained and audited is not deployed; the three tests are conjunctive, and the doctrine is a precondition, not a speed limit.
* **Informed Intent:** no AI system acts without prior authorization stating its purpose, authority, boundaries and exit, given by a human who meets the five authorizer conditions.
* **Final Liability rests with the Human:** every material outcome attaches to a named human owner with decision rights, oversight and the power to intervene.

## 5. Deliverables

The Client leaves with three core deliverables:

* A started AI system inventory.
* Draft risk register entries for the visual inspection and chatbot examples.
* At least two governed workflows.

Supporting drafts include the decision-rights map, the policy section and intake procedure, the governed prompt set, the oversight map, the evidence plan and the three section 8 artifacts. All artifacts are drafts in the repositories. At the close of Day 2, the Client names who owns finishing each one. The program does not certify the Client and makes no promise of an ISO/IEC 42001 or audit outcome.

## 6. Logistics and Price

* **Delivery:** two days, live virtual, four 90-minute working sessions per day.
* **Audience roles:** General Counsel, CISO, Head of Quality, Head of Data, German plant manager and two internal auditors.
* **Dates:** Unknown.
* **Price:** US$12,500. This is within the budget of up to US$80,000 approved for this fiscal year.

**Questions to confirm at intake:**

1. Does the works council need to be consulted before the visual inspection pilot is used as a worked example, even in sanitized form?
2. What data does the chatbot process, and where is it held?
3. Where should working copies of the repositories be held, given that customer data must stay in the EU?
4. Which additional AI systems will participants bring to the inventory exercise?
5. Which time zones should the session schedule accommodate?
6. Should the artifacts anticipate ISO/IEC 42001 work, given that its start date is not fixed?

## 7. Next Step

A decision is expected by 15 December 2026. We propose a 45-minute intake call with Dana Whitfield to resolve the questions above and set dates. The pre-work packet will be issued once dates are confirmed.

Human-made, for Easy Work, Simply Done.
